basics.name: Bernd Accou
basics.label: Postdoctoral Researcher
basics.summary: Postdoctoral researcher at KU Leuven applying deep learning to neural and speech signals. Built the field's largest public speech-evoked EEG dataset (SparrKULee: 168 hours, 85 participants) and the VLAAI EEG-to-speech decoding network; co-organized two international grand challenges (ICASSP 2023 & 2024, 200+ teams combined) and was part of the KU Leuven team that won the NeurIPS 2025 EEG Foundation Challenge. Now extends this work into multilingual, speech-based Alzheimer's disease detection and fMRI signal processing. PhD in Biomedical Sciences (KU Leuven, 2023). 595+ citations, h-index 12 (Google Scholar, Aug 2026).

work.name: KU Leuven — Research Groups ExpORL (Dept. of Neurosciences) & PSI (Dept. of Electrical Engineering, ESAT) & Research Group for Neurorehabilitation (Dept. of Rehabilitation Sciences)
work.summary: Continuing research on deep learning for neural and speech signal processing, multilingual clinical speech AI, Oxcytocin fMRI analysis and co-leading a new KU Leuven-funded project on embodied listening.
highlights: Developed and applied feature-extraction pipelines and multilingual machine learning / deep learning models for Alzheimer's disease detection from speech.
Co-promotor (project co-lead) on 'Objective measures of embodied listening' (KU Leuven, 02/10/2023 - 28/07/2027).

Co-supervising 2 PhD students: one on embodied listening as an objective, multidimensional measure of listening engagement, and one on 'Oxytocin as a Novel Therapeutic Option for Autism: An Exploration of Neuroscientific, Biological, and Patient Perspectives.'

Member of the KU Leuven EEG Decoding Team that won the NeurIPS 2025 EEG Foundation Challenge ('From Cross-Task to Cross-Subject EEG Decoding'), competing against 1,000+ international teams on the HBN-EEG dataset (3,000+ participants); results presented at NeurIPS 2025, San Diego.

Corresponding author, 'Contrastive representation learning with transformers for robust auditory EEG decoding' (Scientific Reports, 2025) — applies self-supervised contrastive learning and transformer networks to EEG decoding.

Co-authored 'A Multi-decoder Neural Tracking Method for Accurately Predicting Speech Intelligibility' (2026), improving objective speech-reception-threshold estimation for populations unable to complete behavioral tests.
Co-authored 'In Sync With Sound' (2025), proposing interpersonal synchronization as an objective measure of listening engagement.

work.name: KU Leuven — Research Groups ExpORL (Dept. of Neurosciences) & PSI (Dept. of Electrical Engineering, ESAT)
work.summary: Doctoral research using machine learning and deep learning to model speech processing and perception in the brain, for applications such as automated hearing diagnostics. Thesis: 'Deep neural networks as a model of speech perception' (promotor: Prof. Tom Francart; co-promotor: Prof. Hugo Van hamme).
highlights: Designed the VLAAI deep neural network for decoding the speech envelope from EEG — the first decoding model shown to work across multiple datasets collected by different research groups, and fine-tunable to individual subjects, substantially outperforming prior subject-specific decoders.

First to predict speech intelligibility from the EEG of unseen subjects in a non-linear classification paradigm, removing the need for extra subject-specific EEG collection (a reduction of 15+ minutes in clinical testing time).

Conceived, collected, and released SparrKULee, a public dataset of 168 hours of speech-evoked EEG from 85 participants — larger than all comparable public datasets combined — now used as a training/benchmarking resource across the field.
Co-organized the ICASSP 2023 Auditory EEG Challenge (42 international teams) and the ICASSP 2024 Auditory EEG Challenge (166 international teams).

Co-supervised 7 completed MSc theses (2020-2022), 1 ongoing PhD student (Biomedical Sciences), 1 ongoing Medical Sciences student, 1 ongoing Audiology student, and ~11 job students assisting with EEG data collection.
Awarded the PhD Quick Pitch Award (Neurotech Leuven, 2022) and the Best Impact Award (CogHear 2023) for organizing the ICASSP 2023 Grand Challenge.

publications.name: A Multi-decoder Neural Tracking Method for Accurately Predicting Speech Intelligibility
publications.summary: With R. Sonck, T. Francart, J. Vanthornhout. Introduces a multi-decoder EEG method to predict speech reception thresholds (SRTs), improving accuracy and robustness of objective speech-intelligibility assessment for populations unable to complete behavioral tests.

publications.name: Contrastive representation learning with transformers for robust auditory EEG decoding
publications.summary: With L. Bollens (co-first author), H. Van hamme, T. Francart (corresponding authors alongside Bernd). Applies contrastive self-supervised learning and transformer networks to learn robust EEG representations; evaluated on match-mismatch classification and envelope-decoding tasks from the ICASSP 2023 Challenge.

publications.name: In Sync With Sound: Interpersonal synchronization as an objective measure of listening engagement
publications.summary: With L. Lambrechts, J. Vanthornhout, B. Boets, T. Francart. Proposes interpersonal (brain/body) synchronization as an objective, multidimensional measure of listening engagement, addressing the limits of purely behavioral assessments.

publications.summary: With C. Puffay, J. Vanthornhout, M. Gillis, P. De Clercq, H. Van hamme, T. Francart. Uses linguistic speech features to classify EEG responses to coherent versus nonsensical speech.

publications.name: Relating EEG to continuous speech using deep neural networks: A review
publications.summary: With C. Puffay, L. Bollens, M. Jalilpour Monesi, J. Vanthornhout, H. Van hamme, T. Francart. Systematic review identifying methodological pitfalls in deep-learning studies relating EEG to continuous speech, aimed at improving reproducibility and statistical rigor in the field; 10+ citations within its first year.

Open-sourced with pre-trained models at github.com/exporl/vlaai.
